copy.caption:
Every house has one room nobody can name. The listing photo has to call it something, and whatever you call it is what the buyer prices.

Empty, that room is a question. We staged the same photograph three times and never moved the camera.

As an office it sells to the buyer who works from home. As a guest room it sells to the buyer whose family visits. As a reading room it sells to the buyer who wants somewhere quiet. Same walls, same window, same floor. Three different buyers.

Go and look at your own gallery. If a room in it has no furniture and no label, the buyer is filling it in for you, and they will fill it in with the version they do not want.

The exterior is the first photo in the listing. It is also the only one nobody restages.

97% of agents told NAR that curb appeal matters for attracting a buyer. Three quarters of them called it very important. Not somewhat. Very.

Then the photo goes up shot at noon under a flat grey sky, because that is when the appointment was.

This is the same photograph. Same house, same brick, same hedge, same neighbour's roofline in the corner. Golden hour and a clear sky, applied as a preset. Nothing was added to the property and nothing was taken away from it except the parked cars and the bins.

That is the whole job. You are not renovating anything. You are photographing it on the day it looks like itself.

The headline was replaced with a number pulled verbatim from NAR's own PDF. The 7% sale-price figure from JREFE was the alternative and was rejected for display size: the paper says UP TO 7% and bundles the seller's curb appeal with the across-the-street neighbour's, which a 280px numeral cannot hedge. The 2018 NAR '87% of buyers find photos very useful' was rejected as stale; NAR's own 2025 figure is 83%. The claim line says agents rather than buyers because that is what the survey measured.

copy.headline: One wall. Nothing else.
copy.caption:
We brushed one wall. The bath, the tap and the towels are the same pixels they were before.

That is the whole of Masking Studio. You paint over the part you want changed, and everything outside the brush is left exactly as it was. Not re-rendered, not redrawn. The original file.

The alternative is restaging the whole photo, and that gives you a new room rather than a new wall. The bath moves. The tap grows a second handle. The light from the window lands somewhere else. It all looks fine until you put it next to the picture you started with.

So here is the check. Run your eye across the seam. The bath rim carries straight through it without a step, and the grout lines meet on both sides. Only the tile changes colour.

We measured it rather than trusting it: of the 118,054 pixels outside the brushed area, zero changed.

One photo. One brush. One pass.

Save this for the next time a client asks what a different tile would look like.

copy.headline: You cannot forget the label.
copy.caption:
Every staged photo on an MLS has to say it was staged. Ours says it before you download it.

Here is the whole job:

1. Tick "Label as virtually staged" in the staging panel.
2. Pick the look. A dark chip, a light chip, text only, or a band across the foot of the photo.
3. Drag the size if you want it louder.

That is the feature. There is no step four.

The tag is burned into the file, not laid over the preview, so it survives the download, the email and the re upload. And if the tag cannot be applied, you do not get the image. That is on purpose. A photo you believe is labelled and is not is the exact problem the tag exists to prevent.

The dining room here is a real render. The table, the chairs, the rug, the pendant and the print were all generated. The room was empty. The tag in the corner went on by itself.

NAR Article 12 and most MLS rules ask for the same thing: if a listing photo has been altered, say so. Nobody is asking for an essay. Two words in the corner is enough.

copy.headline: Put the desk under the window, not against the wall.
copy.caption:
That sentence is the whole prompt. One line typed into the box, and the room below is what came back.

Presets get you a look. They cannot tell the model anything about your room.

This room has one good window and a radiator sitting under it. Put the desk against a side wall and you have wasted the only decent light in the place. No preset has an opinion about that. A sentence does.

So here is what was typed, in full:

"Put the desk under the window, not against the wall."

That is the entire instruction. The Scandinavian preset did the rest: the oak, the white walls, the floor, the plants on the sill.

The room was empty when this started. No desk, no chair, no shelves, no lamp, nothing on the sill. Every object in the photo was generated from one photograph of an empty room and that one line of text.

You do not have to describe a whole room. You have to say the one thing you would tell a stager if you were paying for one.

What would yours say?

Try it on a photo of a room in your own house. Link in bio.

copy.headline: They cannot picture their bed there.

This bedroom belonged to someone. A buyer sees that in half a second, and it is why they keep scrolling.

Nothing structural changed in the photo below the line. Same floral wallpaper, same patterned carpet, same window, same ceiling light. The bed, the wardrobe, the framed photograph, the clothes hanging on the wall and the chamber pot came out, and the room was staged in the luxury preset. Same camera position, same crop.

That is the part worth looking at. The room is not disguised. It is still recognisably the same room, which is what makes the photo usable on a listing rather than a picture of somewhere else.

Buyers do not stall on an occupied room because it is untidy. They stall because the room is visibly still somebody's. Inherited and probate listings are the hardest version of this, and they are also the ones nobody is willing to empty before the photos go up.

One honest note on which half is which. Staging an empty room is free on Stagify. Removing what is already in the room first is a Stagify+ feature, because it runs two passes instead of one.
